Workout Example: A glass flask of volume 400 cm3 is just filled with mercury at 0C. How much mercury overflows when the temperature of the system is raised to 80C? (The coefficient of cubical expansivity of glass is 2.7×10–5 C–1 and that of mercury is 18 × 10–5C–1.)  Solution: Here,  Initial volume of mercury = Initial volume of flask = (V0) = 400 cm3 Initial temperature of system (i) = 0C Final temperature of system (f) = 80C Cubical expansivity of glass (g) = 2.7×10–5 C–1, Cubical expansivity of mercury (Hg) = 18 × 10–5 C–1 Final volume of mercury = V (say) Final volume of glass flask = V' (say) Amount of mercury which overflows (V) = Final volume of Hg (V) – Final volume of flask (V') = V0 [1 + Hg (f – i)] – V0 [1 + g (f – i)] = 400 [1+18×10–5(80–0)]–400[1+2.7×10–5(80 – 0)] = 4.896 cm3=5 cm3 Hence, 5 cm3 mercury overflows.

Sample Questions: 1. Why does a liquid have two coefficients of expansion? 2. The liquid of cubical expansivity  is heated in a vessel of linear expansivity  so that no liquid overflows. Is this possible? 3. Why is it much more difficult to make a precise determination of the coefficient of expansion of liquid than that of a solid?
4. Explain why a column of mercury in a thermometer first descends slightly and then rises when placed in hot water.

When a substance is heated, its temperature increases as well as its volume changes. But mass of the substance does not change with temperature. Hence, as the volume of a substance is inversely proportional to its density for constant mass, the density of the substance changes with temperature as shown in figure 10.13.
